name: French Defense
summary: Answer 1.e4 with ...e6 and ...d5. Learn how to challenge White's pawn center in the Advance, Exchange, Classical and Tarrasch variations, and how to find activity for the c8 bishop.

chunks.title: Introduction: A Supported Central Challenge
chunks.summary: Prepare ...d5 with ...e6, then react to White's choice. A solid pawn chain needs active breaks to avoid becoming passive.
keyIdeas: ...e6 supports ...d5 but restricts Bc8; remember the tradeoff when comparing the French with the Caro-Kann.
Against e5, attack the chain with ...c5. Against exd5, recapture ...exd5 to release Bc8.
Against Nc3, this course chooses ...Nf6. ...Bb4 is the sound Winawer alternative, with different tactical and structural priorities.

plans.white: Use the space to develop and decide whether to advance, exchange or defend e4. Each decision changes Black's targets.
plans.black: Challenge the center with ...c5 and sometimes ...f6 when justified. Find an active role for Bc8 through exchanges or a planned route, not wishful development.

line.note: White claims space in the center.
Prepares ...d5 with pawn support and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal. The cost is restricting the c8 bishop.

comparison.explanation: 1...c6 chooses the Caro-Kann, leaving Bc8 freer but not opening Bf8 yet. ...e6 chooses the French: a different development tradeoff rather than a universally better defense.

line.note: White builds a two-pawn center before Black challenges it.
Attacks e4 with the d-pawn. If White trades, the e6 pawn can recapture on d5, leaving a central pawn in place.

checkpoint.prompt: What was the purpose of ...e6, and what must Black challenge before White consolidates?
checkpoint.answer: Play ...d5 to attack e4 with e6 supporting the d-pawn. A solid setup should contest White's center, not merely wait.

line.note: White defends e4 and develops a knight. Black must choose a system against this supported center.
Develops while adding a second attack on e4, alongside the d5 pawn. White may advance e5 or reinforce the center in another way.

questions.prompt: You're Black. Prepare a pawn-supported ...d5 challenge in the French.
questions.explanation: 1...e6 prepares ...d5 and opens Bf8. Compared with ...c6 in the Caro-Kann, it develops the f8 bishop's diagonal earlier but shuts in Bc8.

questions.prompt: White built the full center. Carry out the central challenge you prepared.
questions.explanation: 2...d5 attacks e4 with pawn support from e6. Delaying this for a random developing move lets White keep both central pawns uncontested.

questions.prompt: White defends e4 with Nc3. Choose the Classical developing move that attacks e4 again.
questions.explanation: 3...Nf6 develops with an attack on e4. ...Bb4 is the sound Winawer alternative; ...dxe4 is the Rubinstein. This repertoire chooses the Classical route.

chunks.title: Advance: Attack the Base of the Chain
chunks.summary: White gains space with e5. Use ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 to pressure d4 rather than defending a cramped position passively.
keyIdeas: The d4 pawn supports e5. Attacking d4 can undermine the advanced pawn indirectly.
...c5 challenges the base of the chain; ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 add pressure, but d4 is not automatically lost.
A knight on f6 would be attacked by e5, so ...Nge7 is a useful developing route in this structure.

plans.white: Use the extra space for piece activity and keep d4 sufficiently protected. Watch Black's pressure before committing to a kingside attack.
plans.black: Develop Bf8, arrange king safety and keep pressure on d4. Consider ...f6 against e5 only when the opened lines will be safe for your king.

line.note: White claims space in the center.
Prepares ...d5 with pawn support and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal. The cost is restricting the c8 bishop.
White builds a two-pawn center before Black challenges it.
Attacks e4 with the d-pawn. If White trades, the e6 pawn can recapture on d5, leaving a central pawn in place.
White closes the center and gains kingside space. The d4 pawn supports e5.
Attacks d4, the base of the pawn chain. Black seeks counterplay instead of waiting behind the e6–d5 wall.

comparison.explanation: 3...Nf6? overlooks 4.exf6: White's e5 pawn directly attacks f6. ...c5 instead challenges the supporting d4 pawn without putting a piece en prise.

checkpoint.prompt: The e5 pawn takes away f6. How can Black challenge White's space without offering a knight to that pawn?
checkpoint.answer: Play ...c5 against d4, the base supporting e5. Undermining the chain is more useful than trying to develop to an attacked square.

line.note: White reinforces d4 with the c-pawn.
Develops and attacks d4 again. The knight is active because the c-pawn has already left c7.
White develops and adds another defender to d4.
Adds pressure on d4 and b2. The queen move has concrete targets, but pressure is not proof of a forced pawn win.
White prepares b4, gaining queenside space and questioning the c5 pawn.
Develops without stepping onto f6, which the e5 pawn attacks. The knight can continue to f5.
White gains queenside space and attacks c5. Black must react to this concrete change in the position.
Exchanges on d4 before White captures c5. Black removes one central defender and clarifies the pawn structure.
White restores material and keeps a pawn chain on d4 and e5. Both c-pawns have left the c-file, so it is now open for either side's rooks.
Moves the knight to an active square, adding pressure on d4. Black should still finish bishop development and king safety.

questions.prompt: White advanced e5. Attack the pawn supporting that chain.
questions.explanation: 3...c5 attacks d4, the base supporting e5. ...Nf6? would put a knight where the e5 pawn can capture it immediately.

questions.prompt: White developed Nf3. Add queen pressure to d4 and b2.
questions.explanation: 5...Qb6 attacks d4 and b2, giving Black targets. The queen may need to retreat if attacked, so this is concrete pressure rather than a general license for early queen moves.

questions.prompt: White prepares b4. Develop the g8 knight without stepping into the e5 pawn's attack.
questions.hint: Use e7 as the first step toward f5.
questions.explanation: 6...Nge7 develops safely because e5 controls f6, not e7. The knight may later reach f5 to add pressure on d4.

chunks.title: Exchange: Free the Restricted Bishop
chunks.summary: After exd5, recapture with the e-pawn. The symmetric pawn structure frees Bc8, so develop actively rather than assuming the game must be drawn.
keyIdeas: ...exd5 opens Bc8's diagonal immediately; the French's usual bishop problem changes.
The e-file is open, but rooks need development and safe entry squares to use it.
Symmetry is a starting structure, not a result. Piece activity and timing still matter.

plans.white: Develop Bc1 and Nb1 and coordinate pressure on the open file. Avoid exchanging automatically if the resulting position favors Black's pieces.
plans.black: Develop Bc8 actively and bring the b8 knight into play. Contest the open e-file and watch for a useful ...c5 break against d4.

line.note: White claims space in the center.
Prepares ...d5 with pawn support and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal. The cost is restricting the c8 bishop.
White builds a two-pawn center before Black challenges it.
Attacks e4 with the d-pawn. If White trades, the e6 pawn can recapture on d5, leaving a central pawn in place.
White chooses an exchange instead of maintaining or closing the central tension.
Recaptures toward the center and vacates e6, opening the c8 bishop's diagonal. Both sides have d-pawns and an open e-file.

comparison.explanation: 3...Qxd5 is legal, but 4.Nc3 develops with an attack on the queen while the e6 pawn still restricts Bc8. ...exd5 restores material and improves the bishop's prospects in one move.

checkpoint.prompt: Which recapture also solves the usual problem of the restricted c8 bishop?
checkpoint.answer: ...exd5 vacates e6 and opens Bc8's diagonal. The same structural problem does not persist in every French variation.

line.note: White develops and prepares castling.
Develops the kingside knight and controls e4. Black uses the simpler structure to bring out pieces efficiently.
White develops toward the kingside and clears f1 for castling.
Develops toward h2 and clears f8 for castling. Black does not need to keep the bishop passive on e7 in this position.
White secures the king.
Black secures the king before occupying the open file.
White places a rook on the open e-file.
Contests the e-file instead of allowing White to use it unchallenged. Neither rook can enter the opponent's position safely without checking defenders.

questions.prompt: White exchanged on d5. Recapture while opening your c8 bishop's diagonal.
questions.explanation: 3...exd5 restores material and releases Bc8. ...Qxd5 is legal, but puts the queen in the path of Nc3 with tempo and leaves e6 restricting the bishop.

questions.prompt: White developed Bd3. Develop your own f8 bishop actively toward h2.
questions.explanation: 5...Bd6 clears f8 for castling and places the bishop on an active diagonal. ...Be7 is sound too, but chooses a quieter square.

questions.prompt: White took the open e-file with Re1. Contest that file with a rook.
questions.hint: Use the rook castling placed on f8.
questions.explanation: 7...Re8 contests the open e-file and prevents White from using it without opposition. Both e-pawns have left that file, so rook exchanges are possible; calculate whether an exchange helps your position.

chunks.title: Classical: Answer the Pin With Development
chunks.summary: After Nc3 and Bg5, use ...Be7 to break the pin, then react to e5 by retreating the knight. A sound position still needs central counterplay.
keyIdeas: ...Nf6 attacks e4; Bg5 creates a relative pin to the queen.
...Be7 breaks that pin and prepares castling. It does not mean White must release the tension.
After e5, ...Nfd7 keeps the knight safe and supports a later ...c5 break. A retreat can serve a useful plan.

plans.white: Finish development and use the space to improve pieces. Check the d4 pawn before expanding further on the kingside.
plans.black: Develop Nb8, pressure d4 with ...Nc6 when available, and seek activity for Bc8. Consider ...f6 only after assessing king safety and central exchanges.

line.note: White claims space in the center.
Prepares ...d5 with pawn support and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal. The cost is restricting the c8 bishop.
White builds a two-pawn center before Black challenges it.
Attacks e4 with the d-pawn. If White trades, the e6 pawn can recapture on d5, leaving a central pawn in place.
White develops and defends e4.
Develops with a second attack on e4.
Pins Nf6 to the queen on d8, restricting its freedom to move without exposing the queen.
Interposes Bf8 on e7, breaks the pin to the queen and prepares castling. Black chooses the Classical line rather than a sharp pawn move.

comparison.explanation: 4...Bb4 chooses the MacCutcheon, counter-pinning Nc3 and accepting sharper tactical play. ...Be7 directly breaks the pin on Nf6 and prepares castling; it is a repertoire preference, not a forced move.

line.note: White gains space and attacks Nf6 with the e-pawn.
Retreats the attacked knight to d7. This preserves the piece and prepares to challenge White's center with ...c5.

checkpoint.prompt: White's e5 pawn attacks the knight you just developed. Does retreating mean Black's opening failed?
checkpoint.answer: No. ...Nfd7 preserves the knight and fits the plan of challenging d4 with ...c5. Useful retreats are part of playing against a pawn chain.

line.note: White exchanges the bishop for Be7, removing Black's dark-squared bishop.
Recaptures with the queen and keeps castling available. The queen on e7 can also support a later ...f6 break.
White reinforces e5 and claims more kingside space, at the cost of exposing diagonals around the king.
Secures the king before changing the central pawn structure.
White develops and supports d4 and e5.
Challenges d4, attacking the base of White's chain. Black needs this counterplay to avoid being squeezed by White's space.

questions.prompt: White pins your f6 knight with Bg5. Break the pin while preparing castling.
questions.explanation: 4...Be7 breaks the pin to Qd8 and develops. ...Bb4 is the sharp MacCutcheon alternative; this course chooses the more direct development plan.

questions.prompt: White attacked Nf6 with e5. Retreat that knight safely.
questions.hint: Return toward d7 to support central counterplay.
questions.explanation: 5...Nfd7 saves the knight and supports a later ...c5 challenge. Staying on f6 would allow exf6, while retreats to the rim are less coordinated.

questions.prompt: Your king is safe and White has a d4–e5 chain. Challenge its base.
questions.explanation: 8...c5 creates central counterplay against d4. Black cannot rely on solidity alone while White develops behind a space advantage.

chunks.title: Tarrasch: Use the c5 Break
chunks.summary: White's Nd2 defends e4 while keeping c3 available. Challenge d4 with ...c5 and learn the activity-versus-structure tradeoff after the central exchanges.
keyIdeas: Nd2 avoids a pin on Nc3 and preserves c3, but temporarily obstructs Bc1.
...c5 challenges the center immediately. The alternative ...Nf6 leads to a different, often closed structure.
After ...exd5 and later dxc5 Bxc5, Black has an isolated d-pawn and active pieces. Isolation is a long-term weakness, not an immediate tactical loss.

plans.white: Use the d4 square as a blockade if possible and pressure the isolated d5 pawn. Avoid neglecting development just to attack the pawn.
plans.black: Castle, develop Bc8 and coordinate active pieces around d5. A timely ...d4 may free the position, but requires tactical support; unnecessary exchanges can make the isolated pawn harder to defend.

line.note: White claims space in the center.
Prepares ...d5 with pawn support and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal. The cost is restricting the c8 bishop.
White builds a two-pawn center before Black challenges it.
Attacks e4 with the d-pawn. If White trades, the e6 pawn can recapture on d5, leaving a central pawn in place.
White defends e4 with the b1 knight while keeping c3 available for the c-pawn. The knight temporarily blocks the c1 bishop's diagonal.
Challenges d4 immediately, using the c-pawn while White's queenside development is less fluid.

comparison.explanation: 3...Nf6 is a sound main alternative and often meets 4.e5 with ...Nfd7. ...c5 instead challenges d4 before the center is locked. Choose the break according to the structure you want to play.

line.note: White exchanges the e-pawn for Black's d-pawn, clarifying the center.
Recaptures with the e-pawn, keeping a pawn on d5 and opening Bc8's diagonal. The queen remains at home.
White develops the g1 knight. The SAN specifies which knight reaches f3 because Nd2 could also move there.
Develops and attacks d4. With the c-pawn already on c5, Nc6 no longer blocks its central break.
White pins Nc6 to the king on e8: d7 has been vacated and the b5–e8 diagonal is clear.
Develops Bf8 toward h2 and prepares castling once the g8 knight moves. The pin on Nc6 still matters until Black secures the king.
White captures c5, inviting a structure with an isolated black d-pawn.
Recaptures while activating the bishop. Black now has an isolated d5 pawn, balanced by active development and central influence.

checkpoint.prompt: After you recover c5 with a bishop, what pawn weakness and piece advantage should shape your plan?
checkpoint.answer: Black has an isolated d5 pawn and active pieces. Castle and coordinate those pieces; avoid unnecessary exchanges that make the pawn easier to blockade.

line.note: White secures the king and prepares to pressure or blockade d5.
Develops the last kingside piece and prepares castling. The knight can help support d5 later, while Black must watch the still-pinned Nc6.

questions.prompt: White chose Nd2. Challenge d4 with the thematic flank-pawn break.
questions.explanation: 3...c5 attacks the center immediately. ...Nf6 is another major response, often inviting e5 and a closed pawn chain. Here we choose direct pressure on d4.

questions.prompt: White exchanged on d5. Recapture with a pawn to open your c8 bishop's diagonal.
questions.explanation: 4...exd5 keeps a central pawn and frees Bc8. ...Qxd5 is also a known Tarrasch line, but requires a plan for the exposed queen; this lesson uses the pawn recapture.

questions.prompt: White took c5. Recover the pawn with the bishop you developed to d6.
questions.hint: Move the bishop one step along the diagonal.
questions.explanation: 7...Bxc5 recovers material and leaves Black an isolated d5 pawn. That pawn can be a target, while the active bishop and open lines provide dynamic compensation. Complete development before trying to prove either factor decisive.
